Who can imagine gallant cavalier
of eye olden time" going to the wars
without waving plume in his cap?
Why, its absence would so entirely mar
the effect that the knight would scarce
ly seem worth ones admiration Long
before the age of chivalry quaint ideas
were eXtant regarding feathers, and
some of our well-known sayings owe
their origin to the waving plumes.


ITO plume ones self comes from
the Hungarians, who placed in their
caps feather for each Turk killed, and
therefore were decorated according to
valor. The use of the white feather as
sign of withdrawal from contest OF
as truce undoubtedly arose from the
the fact that in leaving the field the
white feather to one who intended fight
ing meant usually warning from some
friend that discretion would be the bet
ter part of valor.


The questiyn has often been asked
why the feathers of the peacock, beau
tiful as they are, have the reputation
of bringing bad luck TO the wearer.
The East Indians and the North Amer
lean Indians believe that feathers en-
dow the owner with the vices or virtues
of the bird from which they are plucked,
and rs the peacock is vain. arrogant,
and greedy he can scarcely endow one
with all the virtues. The kingfisher
has been highly honored bird, and to
possess one of his feathers or bit of
the skin has meant great fortune. The
Tartars firmly believe that he who
touches a beautiful woman with king
fishers feather will gain her love.


People who appreciate the beauty of
fine ostrich feathers can imagine the APP
pearance of helmets formed entirely of
them; and yet they were so used by the
ancients without a thought, apparently,
of their ornamental value.


Some old paintings show the artists
love for plumes Of various kinds; the
peacock fans wave before an eastern
beauty, the long white plumes in some
hero's hat, the heron's feather in the
sacy pages cap. while the plume's that
fall far down on white dimpled
shoulders are depicted with the prom
inence they deserve.


Womankind, doubtless. will always

In the meantime the huntSmen had gone great

crop bulletin issued to-day by the Signal
Service for the week ending June 25,
1887, is as follows: During the week
ending June 25. 1887, the weather has
been slightly cooler than the average for
the week, in all agricultural districts
east of the Rocky Mountains, while it
has been warmer than usual on the Pa.
cifc coast. Ia Northern California,
Oregon, and Washington Territory
the average daily excess of temperature
for the week ragged from to 10
degrees. During the week the rainfall
has been in excess in all states ON the
Atlantic coast, along the immediate
Gulf coast, Western Missouri and East
ern Kansas; the heaviest rainfalls oc-
curing along the middle Atlantic coast.
A large seasonal deficiency rainfall
exceeding ten inches continues over the
cotton region and seasonable def.
cheney exceeding five inches exists in
Illinois, Wisconsin and Iowa; in all
other sections the rainfall for the season
differs slightly from the normal. The
weather during the week has been gen.
orally favorable for the principal crops.

doubtless improved the condition of the
staple crop in that region. More rain is
needed in the the cotton region and the
indications this morning are that rain
will occur in the Little Mississippi and


Ohio Valleys by Monday afternoon. The
weather has been favorable for harvest.
ing in the wheat region there having

WASHINGTON, July 10.-The follow
ing is the weather crop bulletin of the
Signal Office for the week ending
July 8. The weather has been
warmer than usual generally through
out the Northern States and on the
Pacific Coast, the average daily excess
being about three degrees from New
England westward to the upper Mis-
sissippi valley and about seven de-
grees on the Pacific Coast. 1t was
cooler than usual throughout the
Southern States and in the cotton
regions the daily average was about
three degrees below the normal.
There has been excess of temperature
throughout the Northern States during
the past two weeks and cool weather
in the Southern States during the
same period. The average daily tenn
perature for the season from January
LIST to July 9th is about normal, the
difference of the daily average from
normal being generally less than one
degree throughout the agricultural
regions.


RAINFALL.


There has been an excess of raiL-
fall in the Southern States and thence
northward to the lakes, including the
southern portion of New England and
the Middle Atlantic States, while
there has been less than the usual
amount of rainfall in the States of the
Missouri valley. For the season from
January LIST to July 9th a large def
cheney of the rainfall continues
throughout the Southern States and
the Mississippi valley, but the rainfall
during the past two weeks has greatly
reduced the seasonal deficiency and,
occurring at the critical period, has
probably effected most beneficially
corn and cotton.


AN IMPROVEMENT.


The weather generally during the
past week has greatly improved the
condition of the growing crops. Both
grain and hay harvesting are we'll ad-
vanced in the extreme northern por-
tion of the country, though they have
been retarded in some sections by Sc
we're local storms.

The two cases of smallpox which came
to light on Wednesday were discovered
bv Chas. Parcels, who went to the saloon
on the corner of Upper Main street and
Bellevue avenue for the purpose of
serving a subpoena, and who walked into
the back room for that purpose.


The origin of the disease is about as
follows: About q month since a man
named Keene came to this city from
Tucson, and shortly after visited the
Lugo family, about nine miles outside OF
the city limits, where there were several
cases of smallpox. He came back TO
this city and was taken down with the
disease, but was hidden by his brother
in house directly opposite the saloon
kept by solomon and Moya. Here he
was found when nearly well, but in some
manner the disease had communicated
itself to Moya's children, who were con-
cealed in back room to the saloon, sep
Hrated from it only by thin partition.
The two children were discovered as stated
by Parcels, but there had been a death
in the family, of child from the same
disease. Health Officer Hagan obtained
warrants for the arrest of Moya and Sol
omon for concealing the smallpox, and
Officer Botello was sent to take the men
to a tent on the smallpox hospital
grounds, where they were kept until
yesterday morning. When the officer
visited the saloon he found trunk
which contained dead child packed in
ice, which the parents stated they were
keeping until they could have it buried.
Officer Botello informed Assistant Health
Officer McAvoy, who procured the am.
bulance and the child was Immediately
buried, it having been ascertained that
it died of smallpox on the same morning.
Solomon and Moya were tried and con-
victed before Justice Austin yesterday,
and both were fined, Solomon $25 and
Moya $50. The Health Officer has care
fully examined the neighborhood and
states that the cases all sprung from the
one man who came here from the Lugo

ing. He then ehoked her with his

rible the crime was, and when

gallery. At present, however, this is
uncertain.


WHEN 1T COMMENCED.


The fire broke out during the first
act of the opera of Mignon. One of the

the entire stage was Immediately
enveloped in flames. The fire soon
spread to the whole house. Madame

we're on the stage when the

out in their stage costumes. The

turned off before all of them left the

soon fell in. sending showers of sparks
as far as the place De La Bourse. With
the exception of Madame Seller, who
persisted, all the actors escaped, though
a number were seriously injured. Five
bodies were terribly burnt.


VAST FURNACE.


In fifteen minutes after the commence
ment of the fire the stage was vast
furnace. Several of the actors escaped
by climbing to the roof on the side of
the Rue Merivantie, where they were
rescued by the fire escapes.


TO REMAIN SEATED.


M. Jasquin inaplored the audience to
remain seated until the exit was opened,
which they did. If they had made a
rush for the doors the loss of life would
have been terrible. The police outside
were unable to restrain the crowd who
besieged the building inquiring for their
friends until military Gordon was
formed. One man, who wanted to res

VIRGINIA CRY, New, June 29.-Noth'
ing has Leen heard from the imprisoned
men in the Gould and Curry mine. The
bottom of the rescue drift is within
eight feet Of connection with the Best
and Belcher drift, where the miners are
supposed 10 be. Drills have been sent
ahead and connection is looked for
every minute. Rumors of all kinds
have been afoat since midnight OF con-
nections having been made, the miners
having been found dead, etc., but there
is no truth in any of them.


WORKING UNDER DIFFICULTIES.


The rescue party expect to reach
the entombed miners tonight, and the
men in the incline are now working
with sponges over their mouths to pre-
vent them from inhaling the gas, which
is coming through the crevices from the
Best and Belcher drift, indicating that
they are liable to break through at any
moment.

text:
The announcement that Russia has
ordered all fertile lands along the
Murghab River to be colonized sounds
strange in this country, where the
only colonists the general Government
orders around are the Oklahoma
boomers. When the Gar wishes to
populate any green spot in his Central
Asian Dominions he orders lot of
Cossacks to pack up their belongings
and be carted off to new homes be-
yond the deserts, that, like sea, di-
vide them from their Fatherland. 1t
must be said that they thrive we'll I'M
der this violent process of transplant
ing. The Government feeds and shell
ters them until they have taken root
in the new soil. The lovely valley in
which Samarcand lies is filled with
well-tilled farms, whose owners are
there simply because" the little father"
shaped their destinies without con-
sulting the humble peasants who did
his bidding. 1t is thus, doubtless,
that the Gar will revive the Merv
oasis, which, irrigated by hundreds of
channels from the Murghab, once
blossomed like the rose.-[New York
Sun.

LONDON, September 16.--A dreadful
collision occurred to-day on the Mid
land railway. A train filed with ex-
cursionists who were going to Dom
caster to witness the races at that
place, collided with another train and
was wrecked. Twenty-four excursion
lists were killed and many injured.


HOW IT OCCURRED.


The Midland train was standing on
crossing mile from Doncaster while
the tickets we're being collected, when
the Liverpool express dashed into it.
The guards box was smashed to atoms
and the first carriage of the Liverpool
train was telescoped by the next. II
was long time before the injured and
dying, who were wedged in the ruins,
could be rescued. Twenty-four per-
sons were killed and many are injured
and cannot recover. The disaster was
caused by defective signalling.

New York, September 16.-The
American yachts Volunteer and May
flower again started this morning to
sail the first of the three trial races
that are to decide which of the yachts
shall defend the American cup against
the Scotch Thistle. The wind was
bowling through the rigging twenty
five miles an hour, and the Thistle,
which was accompanying the two con-
testants, rolled great deal in the
heavy sea.


THE THISTLE OvERMATCHED.
An interesting clinch took place be-
tween the Thistle and the schooner N.
S. Lockwood on the way to the light
ship, in which the Lockwood appar-
emily showed that the Scotch visitors
speed is greatly overestimated. The
Lockwood, at the Romer Beacon, was
a mile and a half behind the
Thistle. She gradually over
hauled the foreigner until
finally, over the bar, both vessels were
sailing on even terms. There seemed
no question but that the Thistle was
sailed for all she was worth. as her
sails were full all the time. The VoluE>
teer crossed the line first, and the
Mayfower three minutes later.
THE VOLUNTEER LEADING.


The Volunteer at IL O'Clock, less
than two hours after starting, was q
little over mile ahead OF the May
flower and Thistle. The wind at the
time was blowing twenty miles an
hour. Fifteen minutes later the Vol
unteer was still gaining steadily on
the Mayfower; the Thistle fast falling
behind.


VICTORY.


The Volunteer won the yacht race
by about two miles,.


THE THISTLE BADLY MANAGED.
The handling of the yacht Thistle in
tO-day's race was of such kind
during the first half of the race as to
give no idea of what she could do.
After that the Scotch yacht was
sailed for all she was worth,
and under the conditions. was
outsailed by both the Mayfower and
Volunteer. The Volunteers time was
hours, 20 minutes and 49la seconds,

ERIE, Pa, November 30--James McLaugh-
lin and Robert Pryor, fishermen, were drowned
about half mile off the shore OF Presque Isle
yesterday. The manner of their death is
remarkable. They started out early yesterday
morning and pulled their nets, making such
large haul that the boat was laden nearly to
the wator's edge. AT this time they were two
miles from shore and the surface of the water
was covered with slush' ice several inches
thick. The men weighed anchor and started
back, but the wind rising caused the boat to
pitch heavily and every lurch caused her to
ship large quantities of semi-liquid ice. Seeing
that it was impossible to reach Erie harbor the
men turned for the Shore but when half
mile out an unusually heavy foe drove large
block of ice into the boat and she slid under,
disappearing from view. The menStruggled in
the water and ice for time but were soon
overcome by the cold, in sight of the crowd on
shore, which could render no assistance.

Associated Press Dispatches to the Herald.
LONDON, September 5.-A theatel
at Exeter took fire this morning dur
ing the performance of "RomaIly
Rye" The occupants OF the pit,
after an awful struggle escaped but
many of them are greatly injured.
There was only one exit from the
gallery, and the crush there was ter
rife. Scores were trodden under foot
and suffocated. The fire escape was
brought to the window and many in
side were rescued. Sixty corpses
have been removed. The mortality is
estimated at one hundred.


ORIGIN OF THE CONFEDERATION.


There are various reports as to the
origin of the fire. 1t is only certain
that the flames broke out in the
scenery shifters department. Those
who escaped say that the special exit
was properly opened. The fire brigade
arrived a few minutes after the break
ing out of the flames but the efforts of
firemen were without avail. There
were several thrilling scenes.


A WEIRD SPECTACLE.


The fire blazed fiercely, lighting the
whole city, and people were soon
hocking to the scene in thousands in
quiring for their friends. The scene
inside the theatre when the fire broke
out was an awful one.


PANIC-sTRICKEN.


Some men implored the audience
to be calm, but it was impossible to
check the frantic mob. The theatre
hose was brought into use in a few
minutes, but had little effect on the
flames. The actors and actresses were
taken from windows with the aid of
ladders. They lost everything except
what they wore at the time.


SIXTY coRPsEs RECOVERED.


Up to the present time 60 bodies
have been recovered; they are almost
unrecognizable. Thirty injured sur
vivors have been taken to the hospital. i.
The fire burned throughout the night
and the search for bodies proceeds
slowly. In many cases every shred OF
clothing is burned off and the bodie
look black and raw.


THIRTY ARE WOMEN.


The majority OF the victims were
men and boys, and about thirty women
were burned. When the fire started
the drop scene was lowered to prevent
draughts, but some OF the actors
opened the door to escape, causing the
fire to burst through the drop scene
and to ignite the gallery.


ROASTED TO DEATH.


The flames overlook the people, who
were wedged in an immovable mass,
and roasted them to death. Many
who were rescued alive died soon after
they were brought out OF the burning
building. The occupants of the dress
circle escaped without serious harm.


HEARTHS MADE DEsoLATE.


A telegram from Exter, at O'Clock
this morning, says that the fire is un-
der control. People distracted with
anxiety are standing about the streets
in the neighborhood of the theater in
search of friends who attended last
nights performance, and the hospitals
are besieged by anxious inquirers for
friends. Twenty badly burned per-
sons who were admitted to the hos
pital died few minutes after they
were received.


ANOTHER ACCOUNT


The structure burned was the Thea
tre Royal, and was built after the
latest designs, and was elaborately
finished, being considered one of the
prettiest in the Kingdom. There was
a full house tonight, and everything
was all right until the end of the third
act, at 10 80, when the drop scene fell,
and in moment the whole stage was


MASS OF FIRE.


A wild panic ensued. The occupants
of the stalls, pit and dress circle
escaped, after dreadful crushing,
many being badly bruised.


THE ACTORS ALL SAFE.


The actors and actresses were in
their dressing rooms when the fire be-
gan and all escaped. The fire origin
ated in the flies and spread rapidly,
filling the theater with dense smoke.
The occupants of the upper circle and
galleries rushed to the windows


SCREAMING FRANTICALLY.


Many jumped from the windows and
were injured and others were rescued
with the aid Of ladders from the
verandahs.

CHICAGO, March l3.-Extreme quiet
marked the burial OF Mrs Neebe to-day.
Fully forty thousand people shivered
three hours in the bleak winds, waiting
for the obseouies of the noted anarchists
wife to commence, and were only re.
warded by a sight of the procession,
that. except in size, differed only in
few minor details from any ordinary
funeral. Last evening the master of the
ceremonies estimated that 90, 900 sympa.
thizers would be in line. Whether the
absence of the anarchist widower damped
the enthusiasm, or the fact that the po-
lice were taking extraordinary precau


tions to quell any disorder, had like
effect, the demonstration fell far short OF
its promoters predictions. Including
persons in III carriages and buggies,
there were probably 5000 souls in the
cortege. The funeral ceremonies were
held in Miller's hall, which, less than
twelve hours before, had been the scene
of masquerade ball. Every vestige
OF the carnival trappings had, now
ever, been carefully removed, and
here and there were placarded
printed appeals for contributions to the
anarchist defense fund. The stage and
gallery-railing were tastefully draped in
black and white, and ranged before the
footlights and around the coffin were
floral emblems and potted plants in pro-
fusion. Nothing symbolical of religion
was visible. After brief orations by
George Schilliug and Paul Groppkan.
the corpse was ready for the hearse.
Neither Captain Black nor Mrs. Parsons
were present. DR.. Schmidt, a socialistic
orator, who has been instrumental in
rasipg large part of the anarchist de.
tense fund, sent letter as substitute
for an address, which he was expected to

red flags, but they were carefully furled

The wedding day was nxed Tor Oc-
tober, and Mark Pendleton returned to
Philadelphia to prepare home for his
bride. 1t was August when he left
Wildhaven, and May had great piles of
sewing to accomplish, but her lovers
parting words were:


Don't work too hard, my darling.
/ want my little wife's face as fair as
spring itself when | come to claim
her."


Before he had been gone two weeks
Wildhaven was thrown into terror
stricken suffering by the breaking out
of contagious fever that spread with
lightning rapidly through the entire
village. 1t was so violent, so fatal
that every one spared actual sickness
was busy in the care of friend or rela'
tive.


May forgot her dainty stitching and
ruffling, her coming wedding, and even
her happiness, in the suffering around
her. In the fearful, scorching heat of
long August drought she worked over
a hot cooking-stove, preparing delica-
cies for the sick, and carried them her.
self to the sufferers, the scorching sun
beating down on her with dry, burn
ing heat Often she found the nurse
of Yesterday the invalid of to-day, and
would remain night after night tend
ing the worse cases under her fathers
care, more than once ending her duty
by dressing the still form of dearly
loved friend for the grave.


Her father guarded her by prevent
tives and precautions as far as possible,
but he never stopped her.


"She is doing the work of her Heav
emily Father; he will protect her." was
his answer to some friendly remon-
strances, and for long time it SEEM
ed as if the maiden bore indeed a
charmed life.


The fever had run its course,
when, in September, cool, wet
week broke the oppressive, heat, and no
new cases occurred afterward except
one. But all, that one tore the doc
tors heart-strings more than all the
rest, for in her room, tossing in
deirious agony, May called pitifully
for the father she did not recognize,
the lover, absent from her, the friends
gone from earth forever Over and
over again she lived the painful scenes
of the past few weeks, and Mrs. Wells,
her faithful nurse, knew she stood
very near the grave for many long
days.


May did not know when Mark PEN
dleton was sent for and admitted to the
darkened room, for what they feared
was last gaze at his promised wife;
she did not know when all the glori-
GUS profusion of her golden hair was
shorn of, to place bladders of ice upon
her head she knew nothing for many,
many days, till, waking from long,
deep sleep, she saw, with clear, COM
pretending eyes, her fathers faco
bending over her.


She smiled, wondering where her
voice had gone, as she said, family;


Father


And he, softly kissing her eyelids, as
they closed again, only murmured;


THANK God! my child is spared to
me-"


There was long convalescence, ana
after May could sit up and be dressed
she wondered where her mirror and
hand-glass had vanished. Mrs. Wells
muttered something about "Eliza's so
careless, always breaking something" "
and her father called her 'little vanity"
with a quivering smile. when she asked
for them.


Even when Mark came, as he did
several times, Mrs. Wells dressed her,
tied on the lace cap that covered her
poor, bald head, and "said sick folks
weren't expected to prink."


But one day, when she felt nearly
well, she stole down to the sitting-room
alone, and looked full in the mirror
over the mantlepiece.


She knew then why she had been so
tenderly guarded from the shock of
seeing her own face. A border of huted
lace replaced her splendid hair, and a
uniform deep pink color was spread
like mask over her whole face. Her
eyes were sunken, and a strange, UNI
natural ugliness seemed to have usurped

SARATOGA, September 2s. The
Democratic State Convention made
the temporary officers permanent and
took recess. Members of the Com
mittee on Resolutions were notified tn
meet at Ex-Governor Dorsheimer's
room at once. Subsequently the Com
mittee on Credentials reported, di-
viding the seats of New York CITY
evenly between the County Democracy
and Tammany. The report was
unanimously adopted. Irving Hall
was left without single representa-
tive.


REVERE THEIR MEMORY.


Before the platform was read eulo-
CYSTIC resolutions in memory of Tilden,
Seymour, Hendricks, Mcclellan and
Hancock were adopted.


A resolution endorsing the admin
istration OF the treasury under Secre-
tary Manning was passed amid great
enthusiasm.


THE PRINCIPLES PROMULGATED.


The platform was then read by ex-
Governor Dorsheimer. The plank re-
lating to workingmen was well re-
ceived. The endorsement of Governor
Hill and President Cleveland was
greeted with tremendous applause,
which continued several minutes,
though that in regard to the President
was the most tumultuous. The planks
relating to civil service, canals, and
liquor traffic was also received with
great applause. The platform was
adopted unanimously.


THE STANDARD BEARERS.


Frederick Cook, for Secretary of
State, and Edward Wemple, for Comp
troller, were nominated by acclama-
ton, and Lawrence j. Fitzgerald re-
ceived the nomination for State Treas
urer. Charles s. Taber was nominated
for Attorney General.


LABOR REFORMS ADVOCATED,
The Democracy of New York
heartily approves the administration
OF Grover Cleveland and eulogizes the
inestimable services rendered by the
Democratic party in reclaiming from
speculative railroad corporations, etc.,
public lands which such corporations,
by the corrupt aid of the Republican
administration had seized, to be dis
posed of for their private gain. The
Democratic party has proved the friend
OF all who come to the country seek
ing to become partners in its welfare
and citizens obedient to its laws. The
remainder of the platform is devoted
principally to State matters. 1t de-
mands that not more than ten hours
should constitute days work, and
the payment of employees weekly and
in money, and advocates legislation
protecting and promoting the interest
and welfare of the laboring classes.


Chase Tabor was nominated for At
torney-General and Jno. Begert for
State Engineer and Surveyor, after
which the convention adjourned sine
die.

SAN Francisco, August 29.-The
United States Circuit Court sustained
the demurrers to the indictments
against John A. Benson and others,
surveyors, who were recently in
dicted for conspiracy in connection
with alleged fraudulent land surveys.


FIELDS OPINION.


Justice Field delivered the opinion,
and said that of the four counts in
each indictment three alleged con-
spiracy and no overt act, and the
other alleged overt act and no con-
spiracy. The Justice said that the in
dictments could not stand, because it
did not appear that ex-Survey or
General Brown had any authority to
laudit or approve any claims against
the United States.


STILL UNDER ARREST.


United States District Attorney
Carey says that the $ rveyors are still
under arrest. He will have new
bonds issued and bring the matter be-
fore the Grand Jury again, at the
earliest possible opportunity.

Across the level tongue OF land from

The tops OF the stones that record the

semblance with the scene; veterans OF
the arboreal growth the scars OF the

screamed from the great guns OF Dahl
gren S monitors and Gilmore's batter
les over this lovely Gods Acre OF the
Southern land; and between the leaf
nge of the sturdy trees the visitor
catches glimpses OF famous old st.
Michael's splre and all the broad and
beautiful vista OF river, city and sea
that extends to the horizon OF the At
antic. 1t is the ancient and venera-

around which Beauregard drew his

so brought the rude and noisy hustle

lasting sleep OF South Carolinians

The western sun battles in golden

uments in this city OF the dead-a

gate beauty OF flowers that bespeaks

MARGARET PICKENS DE ROCHELLE.


DEC. earn, 1864.


When South Carolina seeded from
the Union and lit the fire OF the civil
war her governor was Francis w. Pick
ems, q member OF the slave-holding
aristocracy that boosted OF Its blue
blood, and, like the feudal system Of
men and women. To that rank Gov.
ernor Pickens was entitled, and oil
all the fair and lovable women to
whom his distinguished family had
given birth no one was sweeter Oh
more beautiful than the daughter
who, when Major Anderson lowered
the flag on Sumter. was budding into
a charming womanhood. 1t has been
truly said that the war was prolong-
ed by the courage and persistency
with which the women OF the South
imbued the men. No history has
ever adequately told the sacrifices
that they made, the suffering that
they patiently endured to cheer and
prompt the soldiers and sailors who
served under the banner OF The best
cause. Nowhere between the Poto.

the circus that annually enthuses the small boy
and brings out the bald heads, and like the circus
there is a pronounced sameness in the programme.
do not make this comparison in derogatory

These are the Melancholy Days.-An
exchange puts it this way: The summer of 1887
is dead and gone-gone where the woobine twineth
and the whangdoodle moaneth.


The large and lovely autumn is at hand. Even
now it is getting in its fine work and fancy coors
of red and brown and gold among the woods and
the hills and along the murmuring streams of this
great country.


1t is the time of year when the linen busters and
the Mother Hubbards are put aside with great
gee and warmer garments are brought forth COW
cred with dust and burdened with the odors of
camphor gum and mean tobacco.
The flies that flock together and food the land
in summer time, the blue bottlers and the common
house pest, are going, going, going, and pretty
soon the festive mosquitoes will cease to MARBLE
nightly melodies, swear off and drink no more be-
hind the bar.


The little ant that "provideth her meat in the

gets fat and fatter every day but the gay and
giddy grasshopper that toileth not with her hands,
neither doth she spin, is putting sackcloth and
ashes and getting ready to kick the bucket.


So runs the world. And there you are.


The melancholy days have come,


The saddest of the year:


It's rather warm for whisky straight

She came and went, as comes and goes
The dewdrop on the morning rose,
or as the tender lights that die
At shut of day along the sky.


Her coming made the dawn more bright
Her going brought the somber night
Her coming made the blossoms shine,
Her going made them d. oop and pine.
Where'er her twinkling feet did pass;
Beneath them greener grew the grass;
The song birds rufiled their small throats
To swell for her their blithest notes.
But when she went the blushing day
Sank into silence, chill and gray;
The dark its sable vans unfurled,
And sudden night possessed the world.
o fond desires that wake in vainl
She ne'er will come to us again;
And now, like vanished perfume sweet.
Her memory grows more vague and fieet.
Yet we rejoice that morn by morn
The sad old world seems less forlorn,
Since once SO bright a vision came
To touch our lives with heavenly fame,
And show to our bewildered eyes
What beauty dwells in paradise.

Every pleasant truth you've heard;
Every tender glance and tone,
Every kindly deed you've known;
Every duty nobly done.
Every rightful victory won
Treasure all and count them DER
As a miser counts his store.
But if bitter word or thought
Have bitter harvest brought;
If some foeman hath assailed you,

If unkindness and untruth

Blot the score without delay
Keep no record of the day.

Loss and cross we all must bear;
On the page of memory write
Only what is fair and bright.
Let all evil things go by;
Still, with brave endeavor, try
Simply joys to multiply.
Thus you'll learn how large a sum
Will with faithful reckoning come.
Long as after cloud and rain
Blessed sunshine comes again.
Long as after winters gloom
Summer roses bud and bloom,





One sad heart that we may cheer,

TOMBSTONE, Ari., Dec. 23.-News has been
received from Bonacita that a detachment of
the Twenty. eighth Regiment. under Capt.
Encisco, attacked a band of Yaqui Indians
Sunday morning while they were preparing
to raid the settlement of Laguna del Pars.


After three hours hard fighting the Indians
were driven from their stronghold. One In
dian was killed and one wounded, while two
squaws were captured and sent to Bonacita.
Chico Senaders Qittle Poisoner) one of the
most desperate chiefs in the tribe, led the
Yaquis during the fight.


When forced to retire he covered their re-
treat with skill. The troops
who followed him were ambushed several
times and would have been massacred had
not the Indians run out of ammunition.


Some time ago Capt. Encisco. Lieut..
Oglunin and u squad of twenty five infantry
cred in the hills near Bonacito. The Indians
took refuge behind agranite ledge, and after
repeated charges by the troops the Captain
was forced to retire.


The men were then deployed, but the In
dians broke through the lines and escaped
amid rapid firing. Lieut.. Oglunin was
wounded and the pursuit was abandoned
until next morning. The troops took up the
trail, but did not overtake the fleeing Yaquis.


In this engagement three Indians were
killed and several wounded. While on the
trail II wounded indian was shot dead while
attempting to escape.

COTTAGE Cry, Mass, August s.
To-day was the day set for the sloop-
yacht race. The signal gun was fired
at O'Clock, and the yachts crossed the
line in the following order: Puritan,
Volunteer, Atlantic, Mayhower, Pris-
ella. The Electra steamed after the
fleet in a hurry, and at that time the
Puritan and the Volunteer were APP
parently neck and neck and making
wonderful time.


ENTHUSIASTICALLY GREETED.


Cheers from the steamers and yachts
rang out as the two leaders passed
close under the lee of the Electra and
within one hundred feet of each other.
The start was beautiful, and at
O'Clock every sail had disappeared be-
fore the horizon under a strong breeze
which blew steadily and gave no sign
of tagging out. About five miles from
shore the Volunteer went ahead of the
Puritan in fine style and closed up on
the Sachem, which had come down
with the tide and was leading the
fleet.


NOON REPORT.


At II 10 the yachts were standing
in from Pollock's Rip toward Chat
ham lights, the Volunteer leading and
the Puritan second about a mile
astern.


THE PURITAN's SET BACK.


The Volunteer continued to increase
her lead till out of ght. The Puritan
held her lead over the Mayfower, but
when off Chatham bar she took long
reach off shore, lost her topmast and
was obliged to wear around and thus
lost time in getting clear. Upon get
ting in shore she was behind the At
lantic.


AFTER NINE AND CNE-HALF HOURS.


At = $50 the positions were as fol-
lows The Volunteer, reaching along
the shore on the starboard tack, was
leading the Mayfower fifty minutes,
and gaining every minute. The Pri-
scilla was twenty minutes behind the
Mayfiower, and the Atlantic ten min
utes behind the Priscilla. The Puri-
tan was behind them all, with her
lower sails set. The Sachem was lead
ing the schooners, and the leaders had
all passed out of sight toward Nauzet,
when, at 5 P. NJ, the wind moderated.


LATEST REPORT.


An hour later fifteen yachts, mostly
schooners, were becalmed, with head
tide. None will reach Marblehead be-
fore tomorrow unless a breeze springs
up during the night.

NEEDLES, Cal february IS The per.
sons who were injured in the accident
on the Atlantic and Pacific Railway
by the train going through the burned
bridge on Saturday night were brought
in here last night and everything that
could be thought of was done for their
comfort. Engineer Hodgdon died early
yesterday. His bravery and presence Of
mind in applying the air-brakes and re-
versing his engine saved many lives.
The company had physicians on hand
soon after, and the injured are all doing
well. Express Messenger Thompson.
although injured, worked at the wreck
and saved nearly all the treasure, about
$780, 600. The balance of the express
was total loss. All the east.bound
mail, except four paper pouches, was
rescued. Only two or three trunks were
saved of all the baggage. The remains
of Brakeman Gilbert were picked up and
would not fill candle.box. The fire
man escaped without scratch. Moth
ing remains of the engine and three cars
but mass of old iron. The train did
not take fire till about twenty minutes
after it ran of the bridge, and the flames
came from one of the lamps which ex.
ploded in the mail-car. How the br dge
caught fire no one seems to know. A
track was built around the wreck aud
trains are now running on time. The
wrecked train consisted of seven cars,
containing about seventy passengers.

| HERKIMER. N. Y, February 2S.-


Roxalana Druse, who murdered her hus-


oand, George Druse, in December, 1884,


was hanged for the crime at noon to-
day. Alter services last evening, Mrs.


Druse remained up until about ll:3O.
Deputy Sheriff Manion, with Mr.. and
Mrs. Waterman, were with her. Tho
death watch induced her to lie down.
and she slept about four hours Of quiet
sleep. She awakened with a start. aud
upon arising began to write letters a.
calmly as she had at any time
during her incarceration. In one of
these she thanked the Sheriff for his
kindness to her, and asked that her
body might be given to her sister for
Christian burial. After writing she lay
down again and fell into doze. She
was attacked with hysteria in q violent
form, and it required considerable effort
dpon the part Of the watchers to calm
her. During the night she ale one of the
heartiest meals she had eaten since she
was prisoner. She had about two
hours rest after 4 A. NJ, but did not
sleep soundly at any time. Rev. DR..
Powell visited Mrs. Druse about 8, and
did all in his power to calm her and pre-
pare her for the awful moment. The
execution was witnessed by twenty five
persons, including the officers


Just before going to the scaffold Mrs.
Druse made affidavit declaring that her
daughter Mary, now confined in Onon-
daga penitentiary, had nothing whatever
to do with the killing of her father.


Yesterday morning Mrs. Druse made
confession to Dr. Powell, her spiritual
adviser, in which she declared that
Charles Gates had instigated her to COM
NIT the murder, and that he provided
her with the revolver. She declared
that after she fired the first shot Gates
fired the three succeeding shots from q
window. She confessed to having cut
up her husbands body. According to
her statement Gates took the fragments
away and burned them. She claimed
that she killed Druse because he had
treated her cruelty and brutally.


At ii: :42 Mrs. Druse and DR.. Powell
knelt on the floor Of the scaffold under
the rope. Mrs. Druse held her daugh-
ter's bonnet in her hand, and closed her
eyes while DIR. Powell offered prayer.
The prisoner was dressed in black
cashmere dress, with laced neck and
sleeves. She wore o small shawl over
her shoulders. The woman maintained
her composure on the sc.ffold until the
cap was drawn over her face. Then she
began to moan, and finally screamed 30
loudly that the noise could be heard in
the street adjoining the jail. After the
trap was sprung and she had fallen, she
made but one convulsive movement.

PORTLAND, Ogn., July 12.-News of
a sad drowning accident at Tillamook
has just been received here. Bert
Briggs, who runs small sloop on the
bay, started from Tillamook City on
Sunday with five passengers. When
opposite Jacksonville, the bay being
very rough and a strong Northwestern
blowing, the boat swamped, but Biggs
and Woodruff got on the mud flats and
were rescued by a boat from the can
merry. The other four were drowned.
One was logger from Nestucca, and
the other three were strangers who
had Just arrived from Pennsylvania
and were looking for land. The body
of one has been recovered and the
party is searching for the others. The
names of the strangers are not known.
There are many capitalists from the
East looking through this state for
timber lands, but it is not known
whether the drowned men were capi-
talists or intending settlers.

Associated Press Dispatches to the Herald


SAN Francisco, August 1.-THE
west bound passenger express train on
the Southern Pacific was run off a
switch near Papago about fifteen miles
east of Tucson, A. t., last night by
four masked men, the engine was
ditched and the express car robbed Of
about $500.


SCENE OF THE ROBBERY.


Tho robbery occurred at the same
point where the west bound express
was robbed in April last. On the track
beyond where the train was brought
to standstill the robbers had fastened
three torpedoes to warn the engineer
and compel him to stop his train. The
plan to turn the switch and ditch the
engine was evidently thought of later.


THE RAID BEGINS.


As soon as the train went in the
ditch one of the robbers, who was
upon the bank, commenced firing a
Winchester rifle. He shot twice into
the sleeper and twice through the ex-
press car. The party then went to
the mail car and made the agent come
out and 60 to the express car. They
ordered the messenger to come out,
but he would not open the door. They
then blew the car open with a giant
powder cartridge and forced the mail
agent to go into the car ahead.
ENTERING THE MAIL CAR.


Two of the robbers then went in
and one of them held. route Agent
Gault and the mail agent in one end
of the car while the other covered the
messenger with revolvers and made
him open the safe and put the money
in sack. They struck him over the
head with revolver once, but did
not injure him much.


FOUR IN THE PARTY.


There were four men in the gang, one
was on the bank, one on the opposite
side of the train and two went in
the express car.


They did not allow anyone to come
out of the coaches.


IDENTITY OF THE ROBBERS.


A complety description of the rob-
bers has been obtained and they are
believed to be the same who robbed
the train in April.


REWARD, OFFERED.


The railway and express companies
have each offered $1,000 for the arrest
Of the robbers. Thl train was not
making full speed, and the ditching of
the engine and the following cars kept
the force of the shock from the passen-
ger coaches.


AFTER THE AFFAIR.


Another engine was sent out from
Tucson Immediately and the train
hauled into that place.

WASHINGTON, August 14.-The fol-
lowing is the weather crop bulletin Of
the signal office for the week ending
August 13. In California the daily
average temperature was from two to
seven degrees below the normal. The
average temperature for the season
from January LIST to August 18th has
been generally in excess from the
Alleghanies westward to the Rocky
mountains.


RAIN FALL.


During the week the rainfall has
been slightly in excess in the drought
region, northern Illinois, southern
Wisconsin, southern Michigan, east
ern Kansas, Nebraska, and southern
Minnesota and general rains are re-
ported in the drought region from
Missouri and Iowa eastward to Ohio.
In all other sections the rain fall was
less than usual, except in the
eastern portion of the cotton region.
During the past four weeks, less
than twenty-five per cent. of the usual
rainfall has occurred in Southern and
Central Illinois, Western Kentucky,
Southern Missouri and Northern Ar
kansas. Less than fifty per cent. of
the usual amount of rainfall occurred
in the States of the Upper Mississippi
Valley, and a greater portion of the
rain reported in this section for the
month fell during the past week. In
Western Minnesota, Dakota and Ne
braska, and generally in the States on
the Atlantic coast, there has been an
excess of rainfall during the past
month.


GENERAL REMARKS.


The drouth previously reported in
the corn belt in the central valleys has
been followed by general rains, and
the conditions existing this morning
indicate that rain will continue in this
section; but reports from Ohio, Indi-
ana, Illinois, Missouri, Nebraska and
Kansas state that the rains have come
too late to cause much Improvement in
the already injured crops. The wealth
er has been generally favorable for all
crops in the States on the Atlantic
coast from Georgia northward to New
England and reports from Mississippi,
Arkansas and Alabama indicate that
the weather for the week has been
favorable to the cotton crop, although
the crop needs more rain in portion
of Tennessee and Arkansas.


TOO LATE.


CHICAGO, August 14.-The Farm
ers' Reciew says: Copious rains fell
quite generally throughout the West
last week, refreshing the parched pas
lures and invigorating more or less all
the growing crops. The rains unfor-
tunately came too late to benefit the
corn crop and had no effect for good,
except on the late planted or low ly-
ing fields. Much more rain will be
required to put the pastures in good
fall condition and replenish the wells
and other sources of stock water. Our
estimates having been made from re-
ports prepared previously do not indi-
cate any improvement accruing there
from.

Yesterday morning. at 500 o'clock.
while the north-bound passenger train
was crossing a creek seven miles north of
llillsboro, the track parted, and the
smoker, ladies car and sleeper all turned
somersault over the trestle to the
ground fifteen or twenty feet below the
track. The express and baggage car was
thrown across the track, and The engine
and tender ran on over the ties into the
bridge, the tender leaving the trestle
at the entrance to the bridge and hang
ing over the trestle suspended by its coup
ling with the engine. The bridge was
badly torn and damaged by the engine.


There were about eigteep passengers
in the sleeper, eighteen in the ladies
coach and less than dozen in
the smoking car. All were badly
shaken up, and nearly all
received slight and some very painful
wounds, but none were seriously hurt.
The butcher boy was about the worst
hurt, and it was thought for awhile that
his internal injuries were fatal The col
ored porter had an ugly cut on his head,
from blow which, elsewhere, might have
proved fatal Mr.. Phil Stephenson,
journalist of West Texas, was slightly
bruised up. The wrecking train reached
the place about s o'clock, conveyed the
passengers all back to Hillsboro, aud
then repaired the road 50 the evening
north bound train could pass IL The
wreck all the lamps were eXtinguished,
and the stoves remained closed, other
wise the horror of fire would have been
added to the disaster.


Our informant says many amusing
things occurred, which caused much mer
riment after the first alarm was over. A
poodle dog was sent whirling through
the window, and it was some time before
the bereaved lady found her pet, buried
in the mud outside. Then in the sleeper
Mr.. Gosling and wife, ofNY., occupy
ing one berth, were thrown into a,berth on
the badly frightened male occupant. But
the shock was so sudden that the situa-
ton was not fully realized and Mrs. G..
exclaimed: "Oh, my! There's man in

Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD.


SARATOGA, September 27.-The sum-
mer visitors have all flown and the
event of the day for everybody was
the opening session of the Democratic
State Convention, viii III began at
noon. The famous watering place
presented striking contrast to two
weeks ago, when the Labor Conven-
ton was held. Then the crowd seemed
to be more or less poverty-stricken.
To-day, however, the opposite was the
truth. Silk hats, cigars and gold
watches were everywhere, and evil
dence of money enough and willing
ness to spend were apparent on all
hands. To-day there were a dozen
bands of music and the streets were
gay with splendid marching organiza-
tions.


George Rines, of Rochester, was
unanimously chosen temporary chair
man of the convention. His illusions
to Hill and Cleveland were greeted
with applause.


EQUABLE TAXATION RECOMMENDED.


Resolutions were adopted favoring
the readjustment of the assessment
and taxation laws so that all property
shall ratably share in the support OF
the Government, and thereby relieve
farming and kindred pursuits of the
disproportionate burthens imposed
under the present laws.

Kerry Cows.-The cattle of Kerry are native
Irish breed, indigenous to the mountainous re-
gions, whence their name comes they are very
strong of constitution, their beefis finely marbled,
and their females are valuable for the dairy where
they rank not inferior to any others bred in the
British Kingdom. The peculiar designation of
the Kerry, that she is "the poor mans cow"
clearly defines her capacities, which fit her to
thrive scanty fare, and, though thus faring,
make good returns to the milk pail. Usually
these cows are small; but when we'll fed, they
reach good size, and for the quantity and quail
ity of their milk they are quite invaluable to the
cottage people and the poor tenant holders, of
Ireland. In COLOR the Kerry is black, ordinarily,
with slime. back )" but this is not their only color,
for brown, white and black, and brown and black
ones are found as well. The cows have the points
for the dairy the skin is soft, fine, and yielding
to the touch; its creamy tinge is plain, especially
at the muzzle and the ears, and their escutcheons
are tokens of their quality their horns are fine,
turning upward in piquant way, and their whole
appearance is of exceeding neatness and grace.
American importers have not invested in them to
any extent, which makes them unfamiliar to our
people, but their own good qualities, their thrift
and adaptability, and their geniality in crossing
with the larger breeds, whereby they increase
their fattening propensity-and with the approved
dairy strains-convinces US that their introduce
ton should be furthered and fostered. There is
money in the Kerry COW, whether preserved in the
purity of her blood or changed by out-crossing
She is essentially dairy animal, and there her
intrinsic value is great and broadly exemplifed.

PORTLAND. April 10 Last night the
bridge across the Willamette, connecting
the cities of Portland and East Portland
was finished, and to-day foot passengers
were allowed to cross free. Though the
weather was showery all day, about
twenty thousand people availed them.
selves of the pleasing novelty of walk.
ing across the river. Tomorrow the
bridge will be ready for teams. The
structure is 1854 feet long, not including
its approaches, and the draw spring is
3O4 feet. 1t moves perfectly, opening
in one and tbree-fourths minutes. The
experience thus far indicates that the
bridge will be little obstruction to nsvi
cation. The work was begun in 1852
The piers were built and the approac hes
were constructed when an injunction
was ked for and granted in the United
States court. The injunction was made
permanent and the case carried to the
United States Supreme court. The de-
cision in the United States Supreme
court in the Escanaba case, virtu lily
decided in favor of this bridge and the
Injunction was removed. The work
was resumed last September and pushed
to completion. The Pacific bridge com
pany, O. San Francisco, were the build
ers, and are large stockholders in it.

reached here of an incident which may
involve this government in controversy
with Mexico. Last month the Norwe.
gian bark Brazaleva, went ashore off
Cozumel, Mexico, and the schooner Mel.
lie Blanche sailed from Key West to
render assistance, and found the bark's
cargo had been taken ashore, the vessel
stripped, and everything sold or confis.
Gated by the Mexican authorities. The
crew were held as prisoners, but on what
ground could not be learned. The Mex.
ican custom officers boarded the Blanche,
took her papers ashore and returned
with tie information that the
Blanche could not clear from
Cozumel for Key West, but
must go to Progreso, 240 miles fur.
ther south, to do SO. This morning the
vessel sailed into Key West. The cap.
tain says his crew would not sail the yes.
sci to Progreso. and he brought her to
Key West. As the ship has no foreign
clearance from the Mexican authorities
at the port of departure, the Collector
OF Customs has seized the vessel and re.
fused entry pending instructions from
the Secretary of the Treasury.

John Roop. Harry Neil and Michael Waniko.


The scene in and around the little town after the

hands and weeping for their husbands. whose
mangled bodies lay IN a little clubhouse or snanty

less and dismembered dead horribly mangled and

about on top and beneath che rocks In the quarry.

ately summoned from this place, and the
wounded were properly and promptly cared for.

ties for Prohibition, but even the many country

Nice as most girls are, they are not
of the kind to make matrimony state
of bliss and husbands content with
their lot. For in that thickly thronged
field of girlhood are the peevish and
the contradictions, the selfish and ex-
travagant, the idle and the careless,
the jealous and the unloving,
the stupid and the obstinate,
the flirts who encourage unseemly
attentions, and the future mothers
who will think their children so
many hindrances to pleasure, and
who will not have in their hearts
either human love or animal instinct
for their young. The heaven is not
always pure and blue-howers are not
all perfect and fragrant; and humanity
is like the rest of nature-when beau
tiful and Noteworthy, then most de-
lightful-when hacked and scanned
and marred, then not by
any means delightful! But on
the whole the choice girls
far outnumber those who are not
choice. The elders ofs the generation
may not like this new folly and that
fresh affectation-but those elders
must remember that each new genera
tion makes its own shibboleths,
has its own fashions, and that
youth must needs be foolish, else
it would not be youth at all.
That pump-handle shake is hid.
eous and ungraceful; SO are those
aggressive elbows stuck out at right
angles from the shoulder to the hip;
SO is that silly fashion Of quasi-mas-
culinity in dress; and worse
than foolish is the affectation
of manly thought and free
dom from feminine modesties
of manly license and absence of
feminine restraints. But all this
effervescence will work off in time
and leave the golden liquid clear and
sweet-until another fermentation
sets in, with the same process of run
ming clear when it is over. Our grave
grannies-our sweet mothers-we our
selves, now rannies and mothers to
the present young-have all had the
affectations and follies of youth in
our time. Let us then be patient
with our girls, and lovingly confident
of the noble womanhood into which
they will eventually come.-London
Queen.

WASHINGTON, September 25.-Fol-
lowing is the crop bulletin issued by
the Signal Office for the week ended
September24, 1887: The weather has
been colder than usual in the districts
east of the Mississippi and on the
North Pacific coast, the greatest de-
partures from the normal occurring in
the States bordering on the lower
lakes and on the South Atlantic and
North Pacific coasts, where the daily
average temperature was about three
degrees below the normal. From
Northern New England westward to
the North Pacific coast and in the
South Atlantic States it has been
warmer than usual, the greatest tenn
perature occurring in the central
valleys, where the average daily
excess for the season ranged
from one to three degrees, while
the average daily temperature for the
season near Lake Superior and on the
South Atlantic coast was from one to
three degrees below the normal. Rain
fall in the western portion Of the wheat
region and from Texas northward to
Dakota and Minnesota during the past
four weeks has been abundant, and
generally has exceeded ninety per
cent of the usual amount for that pc
riod. The same conditions will ap-
ply to the belt of country extending
from Lake Erie westward to Iowa.
The rainfall for other sections has
been less than usual, except in the
central portion of the Middle Atlantic
States, the isolated Rocky Mountain
stations and in Oregon and Washing
ton Territory, where it has been
slightly greater than normal. Re-
ports from the greater portion of the
winter wheat region show that the
work of preparing ground is being re-
tarded on account of continued drouth.
Reports from Tennessee, the Middle,
Atlantic and New England States
show that the weather was favorable
for crops, and that the seeding of
wheat is in progress. Reports from
Kansas, Nebraska and the western
portion of Missouri and Iowa indicate
that the weather was favorable to
growing crops. Killing frosts oc-
cured as far south as Central Illinois,
Northern Indiana, Ohio and Michigan
during the latter portion of the week.

PORTLAND, Or, October 3.-It is
learned that the disease known as
"Black Leg" has made its appear
ance among cattle in certain portions
of Baker county, Oregon. Several
large stockmen have lost great
many head already. The disease
principally attacks young, fat cattle,
older ones generally escaping. Active
steps have been taken to arrest the
progress of the disease.


Thus far no clue whatever has been
discovered as to the identity Of the
two men who robbed the stage few
days ago near Auburn, Oregon. De-
tectives have been on the ground, but

ritory, few days ago, and got away

ises to show that the robbery was

men," who must also have been ac-
quainted with the building.

WASHINGTON, July 1.-The weather
crop bulletin of the signal Office end
ing July 80 says; During the week
the weather has been warmer than
usual from the southern New England
and middle Atlantic States westward
to the Rocky Mountains, the aver
age daily excess being about three
degrees. During the week there has
been an excess of rainfall in the
States bordering on the Atlantic and
in the east gulf States, Minnesota, Da-
kota and northern Nebraska. These
excessive rains have been accom-
panied by severe local storms and
result in injury to the growing crops
and retarding the harvest. In the
central valleys and lake region less
than the usual amount of rain occurred
and the drought continues in the
corn belt extending from Ohio west
ward to Iowa and Kansas. During
July the rainfall was generally in ex-
cess in the States on the Atlantic
coast. Throughout the cotton belt
in the extreme northwest and
portions Of the Upper Lake Region
there has been less than the usual
amount of rain during the month, and
probably less than one-half the usual
amount throughout the corn belt. The
excessive heat and absence of rain
through the corn belt has effected this
crop unfavorably, and reports from
Ohio, Michigan, Indiana and thence
westward to Kansas indicate that the
drought has unfavorably effected pota-
toes and the corn crop. In the Mid
die, Atlantic and New England States
the weather has been unfavorable to
the corn, and excessive rains have in
jured hay and oats. In Minnesota,
Dakota and Nebraska the weather has
been generally favorable to all crops.
Harvesting is in progress as far north
as the 47th parallel.

returned short time ago and reported

Fort Wingate, New Mexico, crossing

Phoebe, Tho and Owens Crossing in
in the Sierras, through Kings Pass,

had seen that her grandmother was a
bad woman. The boy who is nine
years old was also questioned. He
said that he wanted to live with his
sister, and further than this he did
not appear to have any interest in the
proceedings.

The well-known traveller, NJ. Ed.

esting study of the native inhabitants
of Luzon, the largest and most I'M.
portant OF the PHILIPPINE Islands.


They are divided into two races, the
negritos and the savages, altogether
comprising some fifteen tribes, more
or less distinct in type and costume.
The negritos, supposed to be the
aborigines, are dwarfs, averaging
about four and half feet in
height, but are we'll formed.
Huts or villages are unknewn
among them, but they sleep where
night finds them. Their strongest
characteristic is their love of freedom.
When one of their number dies they
attribute it to some evil influence, and
avenge the dead by killing some per-
son OF another race, and are con-
stantly at war among themselves and
with the savages. These differ in
most respects from the negritos.
Their toes are very far apart and are
used like fingers, they being able to
pick up the smallest thing



with them. Some have even been
seen to descend a tree head fore
most, using their hands and feet
like monkey. They have all some
idea of supreme being, one tribe
worshipping god who had two sons
and two daughters, from whom de-
scended the human race. They defy
such things as the rain, powder, the
metals and certain trees, as wells as
truth and noble deeds. They have
bad spirits, also, as darkness, lying
and some diseases, but neither good
nor bad have any sacred places.
"What need of temples" say they,
ssfor beings who fear neither wind,
sun nor rain?" They chafe under the
Spanish yoke and praise the apes for
their cunning, saying: They do not
speak for fear of being obliged TO pay
axes. ."--fNew York Post.
